publication_scope.blurb: Ludwig Crocius — Book I Chapter 5 On Sacred Scripture's perfection and sufficiency, from the 1636 Bremen Latin. Densify COMPLETE (PHYS 210–mid-238): perfection defined so nothing may be added or subtracted; three heads (canonical number; authentic-text purity; integrity of lettering / vowel-points); what Scripture contains as necessary; thirteen reasons for perfection; three contradictions (papal traditions; zealots of private consequences; diverting the Church from the Bible); two modes of containing revelation. Cap. 6 On Scripture's clarity begins mid PHYS 238; Cap. 4 complete; the rest of the Syntagma remains.
publication_scope.era_note: Crocius wrote in the early seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the illustrious school of Bremen. This is not a patristic work. source_text: CAPUT QUINTUM. De sacrae Scripturae perfectione & sufficientia. Hactenus de sacra Scripturae authoritate: sequitur perfectio, quae est illius proprietas, qua catholica principia doctrinae sacrae omnibus Christianis communia & necessaria partim Hebraica, partim Graeca lingua integre & pure proposita, tam sufficienter complectitur, ut nihil addi, nihil subtrahi debeat. Deut. 4.2. Prov. 30.6. 2 Cor. 2.17. Apoc. 22.18.19. Sic & Aristoteles lib. 2. de caelo cap. 4. perfectum definit, cui nihil deest & extra quod nihil eorum quae sunt ejus accipi potest. Et hoc exigit ratio canonis, qui Varino finitore est μέτρον καὶ κριτήριον, mensura infallibilis, nullam admittens additionem aut deminutionem. Haec sacri canonis perfectio certa est, 1. quantum ad librorum canonicorum numerum, 2. quantum ad textus authentici puritatem, 3. quantum ad literaturae integritatem.
english:
CHAPTER FIVE
On Sacred Scripture's perfection and sufficiency

So far concerning Sacred Scripture's authority: next comes perfection, which is its property by which the catholic principles of sacred doctrine common and necessary to all Christians, set out wholly and purely partly in the Hebrew tongue and partly in the Greek, are so sufficiently embraced that nothing ought to be added and nothing subtracted ([[Deuteronomy 4:2 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 4:2]]; [[Proverbs 30:6 >> Bible:Proverbs 30:6]]; [[2 Corinthians 2:17 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 2:17]]; [[Revelation 22:18 >> Bible:Revelation 22:18]]-[[Revelation 22:19 >> Bible:Revelation 22:19]]).

So also Aristotle, On the Heavens book 2 chapter 4, defines the perfect as that to which nothing is lacking and outside which nothing of the things that belong to it can be taken. And this the nature of a canon requires, which Varinus defines as μέτρον καὶ κριτήριον — an infallible measure admitting no addition or diminution.
This perfection of the sacred canon is certain (1) as to the number of canonical books, (2) as to the purity of the authentic text, (3) as to the integrity of the lettering.

source_text: XIV. Tertio, contradicunt ipso facto omnes, qui, non officii & ecclesiae singularis necessitate compulsi, sed vulgari scribendi prurigine concitati, jam inde a tempore Apostolorum, omissa charitate prima sive praxi sanctorum, sacris literis plenissime descripta, Ecclesiam Christi πολυλογίᾳ sua ab opulentissimo saluberrimoque Bibliorum penuario ad penuriam & maciem voluminum suorum in hodiernum misere avertunt. Nam sacra, quae hodieque appellamus, BIBLIA sunt unicus ille, ditissimus, sufficientissimusque liber & canon, qui, ceteris cunctis in spongiam aut pyram abeuntibus, solus plus quam sufficiens est ad Dei cultum, hominumque salutem, etiamsi humano digito ne minimus quidem apex apponatur; si modo sanctorum praxis vera & Apostolica, & laboriosa charitas fidei pietatisque Christianae, libro isto saturatis coloribus & graphice satis depicta, loco tot glossarum, exegesum, interpretationum, disputationum, commentationum, conciliationum, dilucidationum, summarum, locorum communium, catechesium, Articulorum, symbolorum, conciliorum, confessionum, postillarum, similiumque librorum, quorum nec modus, nec finis est, & sub quorum onere orbis Christianus ingemiscit, ab Ecclesiarum episcopis & curatoribus, Christianis magistratibus, omniumque ordinum hominibus, cupidis aeternae salutis, jure postliminii in usum revocetur. Si enim pii historiarum & controversiarum ecclesiasticarum peritiam, qua pollent, consultent, dubio procul deprehendent, non alia potiore de causa, quam ob omissionem charitatis primae, Apoc. 2.4. iram Dei, moto candelabro ecclesiae novi Testamenti sub Smyrnenfi, Pergamenfi, Thyatirenfi & Sardenfi nostra conditione tam graviter incumbere, ut vix major inter has periodos & Ephesinam, in qua ipsi Apostoli docuerunt, similitudo sit, quam inter agnos & catulos, dum pro vera & practica Dei notitia, qua Apostolica ecclesia collustrata fuit, merae haereses, earumque refutationes, verborum pugnae & scholarum rixae, sub quibus, hac fidei efficacia & praxi pietatis magis atque magis deficiente, merissimae humanarum opinionum inaniae tantopere invaluerunt & oppleverunt omnia, ut ipsa lux divinarum literarum tam tenebricosa, obscura & insufficiens judicata fuerit, & Christianorum primicerii, more Israelitarum super Baalim, Domini propemodum obliti, a mortuis vitam & a tenebris, sive Papae, sive suis lucem petere plerique coeperint. XV. Ceterum, revelata sacris literis duobus modis continetur: uno modo αὐτολεξεί, secundum rem nobis signatis verbis expressam: altero vero δυνάμει, secundum rem non tamen signatis verbis expressam. PRIOR modus, ut habet verba ὑγιαίνοντα & sana, 1. Tim. 6.3. ita quoque observanda sunt & in iis regula Apostoli tenenda 2. Tim. 1.13. quoniam, etsi teste August. lib. 10. de civ. Dei, cap. 23. liberis verbis loquuntur philosophi, nec in rebus ad intelligendum difficillimis offensionem religiosarum aurium pertimescunt: nobis tamen ad certam regulam loqui fas est, ne verborum licentia etiam de rebus, quae his significantur, impiam gignat opinionem. Posterior vero modus habet verba, quae si ab ecclesia noviter adhibentur, ut iisdem non-dicta res exprimatur, repudianda non sunt, modo res iis significata sit εἰς γράμματα in literas relata. Hujusmodi res est Trinitas, ὁμοούσιον personarum trium deitatis: de qua Augustinus tract. 97. in Johan. ita disserit. Adversus impietatem Arianorum haereticorum novum nomen Homousion patres condiderunt, sed non rem novam tali nomine signaverunt. Hoc enim vocatur Homousion, quod est: Ego & pater unum sumus, unius videlicet ejusdemque substantiae. Utro vero modo Deus revelet dogma aliquod, ad veritatem & infallibilitatem nihil interest, cum constet utrumque a Spiritu sancto vere haberi. Ne vero quis turbetur ambiguitate αὐτολεξεί, duobus modis accipitur. 1. Rhetorice, atque ita idem est, quod literaliter proprium, cum vox quaedam proprie & non modificaté sumitur & tropice opponitur. 2. Hermeneutice, atque ita idem est, quod literaliter expressum, cum dogmatis aut rei cujusdam vox, qua signatur, in sacris habetur, utro id fiat significatu: quomodo asserimus, multa esse credenda, quae non sunt αὐτολεξεί ῥητῶς disertis verbis scripta, modo res ipsa sit in Scripturis: ad quam eliciendam ἔντεχνῳ συλλογισμῷ vera ratiocinatione opus esse patres jam olim judicarunt.
english: XIV. Third, all contradict by the very deed who, not compelled by duty and the singular necessity of the Church, but stirred by the common itch of writing, already from the time of the Apostles onward, all first love — or the practice of the saints fully described in the sacred letters — set aside, miserably turn the Church of Christ by their πολυλογία from the richest and most wholesome storehouse of the Bibles to the poverty and leanness of their own volumes to this day.

For the sacred Bibles, which we still call so, are that one richest and most sufficient book and canon which, all the rest going into sponge or pyre, alone is more than enough for the worship of God and the salvation of men, even if not the least apex is set to it by a human finger — if only the true and apostolic practice of the saints, and the laborious charity of Christian faith and piety, painted in that book in full colors and graphically enough, is recalled by right of postliminium into use by the bishops and curators of the churches, by Christian magistrates, and by men of every order desirous of eternal salvation, in place of so many glosses, exegeses, interpretations, disputations, commentaries, reconciliations, elucidations, summas, commonplaces, catechisms, Articles, symbols, councils, confessions, postils, and like books, of which there is neither measure nor end, and under whose burden the Christian world groans. For if the pious consult the skill in church histories and controversies which they possess, they will without doubt discover that for no better cause than the omission of first love ([[Revelation 2:4 >> Bible:Revelation 2:4]]) the wrath of God, the candlestick moved, so heavily presses upon the church of the New Testament under the Smyrnaean, Pergamene, Thyatiran, and our Sardian condition, that scarcely greater likeness remains between these periods and the Ephesian, in which the Apostles themselves taught, than between lambs and pups — while in place of the true and practical knowledge of God with which the apostolic church was lit, bare heresies and their refutations, fights of words and quarrels of the schools have so prevailed, the efficacy of faith and the practice of piety more and more failing, that the light of the divine letters itself has been judged so dark, obscure, and insufficient, and the foremost of Christians, after the manner of the Israelites over the Baals, almost forgetting the Lord, have mostly begun to seek life from the dead and light from darkness — whether the Pope's or their own.

XV. For the rest, what is revealed in the sacred letters is contained in two ways: one expressly (αὐτολεξεί), according to the thing expressed to us by the signed words; the other virtually (δυνάμει), according to the thing though not expressed in signed words. The former mode, as it has sound words ([[1 Timothy 6:3 >> Bible:1 Timothy 6:3]]), so those words must also be kept and the Apostle's rule held in them ([[2 Timothy 1:13 >> Bible:2 Timothy 1:13]]) — since, though Augustine witnesses (City of God 10.23) that philosophers speak with free words and do not fear offense to religious ears in things hardest to understand, yet it is right for us to speak by a fixed rule, lest license of words also beget an impious opinion about the things signified by them.

But the latter mode has words which, if newly employed by the Church so that by them a thing not so spoken may be expressed, must not be repudiated, provided the thing signified by them is brought into the letters. Of this kind is the Trinity, the Homoousion of the three persons of the Godhead — of which Augustine treats thus (tract. 97 on John): Against the impiety of the Arian heretics the fathers coined the new name Homoousion, but they did not signify a new thing by such a name. For this is called Homoousion which is: I and the Father are one — namely of one and the same substance. But whichever way God reveals some dogma, it makes no difference as to truth and infallibility, since it is agreed that both are truly had from the Holy Spirit. And lest anyone be troubled by the ambiguity of αὐτολεξεί, it is taken in two ways. First, rhetorically, and so it is the same as literally proper, when a certain word is taken properly and not modified and is opposed to tropically. Second, hermeneutically, and so it is the same as literally expressed, when the word by which a dogma or some thing is signed is had in the sacred writings, in whichever signification that is done — which is how we assert that many things must be believed that are not written in so many express words, provided the thing itself is in the Scriptures: to elicit which the fathers long ago judged that a true reasoning is needed.

source_text: 7. Absurda est: quia, stante punctorum novitate, sensus Scripturae maxime dubius est, id quod cum Dei loquentis veritate, simplicitate & immutabilitate pugnat & uni simplici sacrae Scripturae dicto plures literales sensus, ac proinde dubios, affingit, id quod tribus modis probatur. 1. Confessione eorum, qui punctorum novitatem defendunt. Auctor Arcani revel. punct. l. 2. cap. 22. Si, inquit, proferantur nonnulla Scripturae loca, in quibus varia punctatio varium quidem gignit sensum, sed utrumque verum, commodum, aptum, antecedentibus & consequentibus non male cohaerentem, analogiae fidei non repugnantem, quid hic erit periculi, si hic hanc punctuationem & cum punctuatione sensum, alius aliam punctuationem & alium cum punctuatione sensum amplectatur? Aut quid periculi etiam fuerit, si utrumque qui ex ea exsurgit sensum? Nullum equidem. Et Rabi Bechai super Num. 11.15. Consone, ait, sine punctis vocalibus varias & ornatas intelligentias habent, qua de causa praeceptum habemus de non addendis vocalibus libro legis, quod unicum duntaxat sensum haberent: sine ipsis vero varias & miras significationes admittunt. 2. Ratione. Sicut enim ex determinatione subjecti & praedicati per copulam fit unum enunciatum: ita ex punctuatione vocum textus Hebraici fit ad unum sensum determinatio, quae, omissa illa, saepe dubia est. Hinc Münsterus: Qui non advertit quod supra infraque in libris scribitur, is pervertit verba Dei viventis. Et ex Racanati: Certum est, quando litera non punctatur, posse vario legi modo; quando vero habent puncta adjecta, unum duntaxat prae se ferunt sensum, juxta punctuationis formam. Quare puncta una cum 22. literis ab auctore simul, aut Scriptura olim cerei instar mollis nunc in hanc partem, nunc in illam fuit flexibilis. Et si puncta ab hominibus sunt inventa, sequitur necessario, Scripturam hoc nostro tempore auctoritatem habere, non divinam, id quod absurdissimum est. 3. Exemplis, quae vide apud Engelbertum praefatione in Lexicon pentaglottum Schindleri. Cetera, distinguendum est inter authentica & publica Biblia & privata. Illa antiquitus non fuisse punctata, nondum firmiter satis probatum est: haec non omnia esse punctata concedimus. Ut enim haec punctis carerent, fecit rei difficultas: ut illa non carerent, fecit religionis necessitas, teste Franc. Junio in animadv. Bellarm.
english: (7) It is absurd. For if the novelty of the points stands, the sense of Scripture is most doubtful — which fights against the truth, simplicity, and immutability of the speaking God, and foists on one simple saying of sacred Scripture several literal senses, and therefore doubtful ones. This is proved in three ways.

First, by the confession of those who defend the novelty of the points. The author of the Arcanum of revealed punctuation (book 2, chapter 22) says: If some places of Scripture are brought forward in which varying pointing begets a varying sense, yet each true, fitting, apt, not badly cohereing with what goes before and after, and not against the analogy of faith — what danger will there be if here one embraces this pointing and with it this sense, another another pointing and another sense with it? Or what danger even if both senses that rise from it? None, he says. And Rabbi Bechai on [[Numbers 11:15 >> Bible:Numbers 11:15]]: Consonants, he says, without vowel points have various and ornate understandings; for which cause we have a precept not to add vowels to the book of the Law, because they would then have only one sense — whereas without them they admit various and wonderful significations.

Second, by reason. For as from the determination of subject and predicate by the copula one statement is made, so from the pointing of the words of the Hebrew text there is a determination to one sense, which, that pointing omitted, is often doubtful. Hence Münster: He who does not heed what is written above and below in the books perverts the words of the living God. And from Recanati: It is certain that when a letter is not pointed it can be read in various ways; but when points are added it bears only one sense, according to the form of the pointing. Therefore either the points together with the twenty-two letters are from the Author at once, or else Scripture was once flexible like soft wax, now this way, now that. And if the points were invented by men, it necessarily follows that Scripture in this our time has authority that is not divine — which is most absurd.

Third, by examples, which see in Engelbert's preface to Schindler's Pentaglot Lexicon. For the rest, one must distinguish between authentic and public Bibles and private ones. That the former were of old unpointed has not yet been firmly enough proved; that the latter were not all pointed we grant. For as difficulty made these lack points, so necessity of religion made those not lack them — witness Franciscus Junius in his Animadversions on Bellarmine.

source_text: 3. Periculosa est, 1. quia citra necessitatem tum temporis illa mutatio Bibliorum facta foret, siquidem facta est: cum quia Deus providentia sua scripturam sacram quam eousque conservarat in sera usque secula sine tali additamento conservare potuisset, tum quia eos neque mandatum Dei neque ulla necessitatis ratio ad hoc opus adegit. Nam auctor Arcani punctuationis revelati lib.1. cap.18. multis rationibus demonstrat quod & quodammodo Hebraica non punctata legi olim potuerint, & hodie e Judaeorum M.S. scimus ipsos sine punctis quam expeditissime sacros textus legere. 2. quia hactenus a tot retro seculis in authentico Bibliorum textu illud fuisset quod omni ex parte verum non est, neque ad authentiae majestatem pertinet. Nam cum anonymus auctor lib.2. cap.22. docet judicium nostrum in puncta illa ultimo & infallibiliter figi non posse, neque e veritate sensus qui ex illa punctorum positura & forma hodie oritur infallibiliter & authentice quicquam concludi debere — ruit & Empusae ad instar in auras abit quod adhuc habitum est pro eo quod ad authentici textus integritatem literariam pertineat. 3. quia ita dubium erit quidnam Spiritus sanctus proprie intenderit in singulis scripturae locis, nosque id infallibiliter scire non poterimus. Nam ad puncta quibus hodie utimur tanquam ad authentiae asylum confugere non licet, quia nova sunt, & negatur ex iis emergentis sensus infallibilitas. Neque enim punctatores prophetas fuisse crediderit, cum Rabinos Christiani nominis hostes infestissimos fuisse constet. Neque interibi ad literas provocare satis est: cum enim hae informes sint, unde sibi formam infallibilem allicient? Confugiendum erit ad magistrum vivum aut mutum: ille non datur & si daretur fallibilis foret; hic in hodiernum desideratur. Paraphrasis Chaldaica versionest non authentia; tenebrae Rabinorum barathrum nugarum; synagoga post ascensum Christi nulla est — hac ratione genuinus sensus unice penderet ab ecclesia Judaica, & scriptura foret litera mortua.
english: (3) It is dangerous. First, because that change of the Bibles would have been made without necessity of the time, if it was made at all: both because God by His providence could have preserved the sacred Scripture He had kept until then into late ages without such an addendum, and because neither God's command nor any reason of necessity drove them to this work. For the author of the Arcanum of punctuation revealed (book 1 chapter 18) shows by many reasons that unpointed Hebrew could somehow be read of old, and today we know from Jewish manuscripts that they read the sacred texts most readily without points.

Second, because for so many ages back that would have stood in the authentic text of the Bibles which is not true in every part and does not belong to authenticity's majesty. For when the anonymous author (book 2 chapter 22) teaches that our judgment cannot finally and infallibly be fixed on those points, and that nothing ought to be concluded infallibly and authentically from the truth of sense that arises today from that placement and form of the points — then what has until now been held as belonging to the authentic text's literary integrity collapses and vanishes into air like an Empusa.

Third, because it will then be doubtful what the Holy Spirit properly intended in each place of Scripture, and we will not be able to know it infallibly. For we may not flee to the points we use today as to authenticity's asylum, because they are new, and the infallibility of the sense emerging from them is denied. Nor would one believe the punctators were prophets, since the rabbis are known to have been the fiercest enemies of the Christian name. Nor is it enough meanwhile to appeal to the letters: since these are formless, from where will they draw an infallible form? One will have to flee to a living or mute master: the former is not given, and if given would be fallible; the latter is wanting to this day. The Chaldee paraphrase is a version, not authenticity; the rabbis' darkness is a gulf of trifles; after Christ's ascension there is no synagogue — on that path the genuine sense would hang solely on the Jewish church, and Scripture would be a dead letter.

source_text: XIII. Secundo, contradicunt zelotae quidam non in fide charitatis, in quibus nullus zelus est nimius, sed in scientia, h.e. in iis controversiis, in quibus facile etiam pii quandoque errare possunt: qui interpretationibus & consequentiis quibusdam suis, quamvis notorie in Ecclesia omni tempore non receptis, aeque ac Dei verbo credi postulant. Hi tales, etsi a Papatu secessionem fecisse videri volunt, salva hac opinione sua, solas Scripturas perspicuum ac sufficientem fidei canonem esse, contra Pontificios tueri vix possunt: si videlicet necessario credi volunt, quicquid ipsi interpretatione & consequentia non catholica illa, & concessa ab omnibus, sed controversa & quibusdam tantum doctoribus peculiari ex Scripturis confidunt certo deduci posse. In omni enim consequentia aliquid rationis assumitur ad testimonium expressum in Scripturis. Assumtum autem illud naturale, nisi sit commune omnium piorum, vel etiam omnium sanorum hominum, & sic inter illos piorum quoque, non est certo aliquid & notorie divinum, aequipollens & quasi in Scripturis subintellectum, sed ad τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου elementa mundi pertinet, Col. 2.v.8. Addunt igitur Scripturis, qui hoc utuntur, eaque re ad novas quotidie haereses fingendas decumanam portam omnibus aperiunt. Nemo enim erit, qui non suam aliquam argumentationem necessariam atque evidentem esse existimet.
english: XIII. Second, certain zealots contradict — not in the faith of charity, in which no zeal is too little, but in knowledge, that is, in those controversies in which even the pious can sometimes easily err — who demand that their interpretations and certain consequences, though notoriously not received in the Church in every age, be believed equally with the Word of God.

Such men, though they wish to appear to have made a secession from the Papacy, can scarcely, while this opinion of theirs stands safe, defend against the papists that the Scriptures alone are the clear and sufficient canon of the faith: namely if they will that whatever they themselves, by an interpretation and consequence not that catholic one granted by all, but a controversial one peculiar only to certain doctors, think can certainly be deduced from the Scriptures, must necessarily be believed. For in every consequence something of reason is assumed toward the testimony expressly in the Scriptures. And that natural assumption, unless it is common to all the pious, or even to all sound men, and so among them to the pious too, is not certainly and notoriously divine, equipollent and as it were understood under the Scriptures, but belongs to the στοιχεῖα καὶ κόσμου — the elements of the world ([[Colossians 2:8 >> Bible:Colossians 2:8]]). Those who use this therefore add to the Scriptures, and by that very thing open a gaping gate to all for inventing new heresies daily. For there will be no one who does not think some argumentation of his own to be necessary and evident.
